text: Only the indicative fixes time.

It lives in the principal parts of a few hundred verbs, and the commonest of those you will meet often enough to learn without trying.
The endings are shared in most tenses, so only the verb and the sentence can settle it.
Principal parts Each verb has up to six principal parts — the building blocks every other form is made from: present, future, aorist active, perfect active, perfect middle/passive, aorist passive.
The discipline From here on, never say a form means something until you have parsed it.
Only in the indicative.

text: Four prepositions worth meeting now A preposition tells you how its noun relates to the rest of the sentence, and in Greek it fixes that noun's case.
Dative, always.
ὁ μαθητής , never ἡ μαθητής .
It is one of the few accent rules worth learning as a rule, because it never varies and it identifies the form on sight.
ἐν, εἰς, ἐκ and ἀπό each take one case only, which makes them the most reliable case signposts in the text.
The vowel depends on the letter before it, and the rule is worth knowing because it decides two of the four singular endings.
The genitive plural always has a circumflex Every first-declension noun ends its genitive plural in -ῶν , with a circumflex, wherever the accent falls in the rest of the word.
None of this changes the meaning or the case.
Where the noun has no article, nothing decides it for you and the context is all you have — which is the same limit chapter 21 will reach with participles.
The article, and only the article.
This is why compound verbs are awkward to look up: the form no longer begins with the letters the lexicon lists.
ἔλυον is first singular or third plural, and you cannot tell from the word.
If it begins with a long vowel or a long diphthong there is nothing left to lengthen, so the past looks exactly like the present.
This is what makes compound verbs awkward to look up, because the form on the page no longer starts with the letters the lexicon lists.
Two past tenses, and the difference between them is not when the action happened.
εὑρίσκω keeps its εὑ- throughout, and the ending is then the only thing telling you the tense.
Only that it is viewed as a whole, from outside.
Its past is the imperfect: ἤμην, ἦς, ἦν, ἦμεν, ἦτε, ἦσαν — and ἦν alone accounts for most of its 455 occurrences.

If the verb already begins with a short vowel, that vowel lengthens instead of taking a prefix: ἀκούω → ἤκουον .
εὑρίσκω keeps its εὑ- throughout, so the ending is the only thing distinguishing the imperfect from the present.
And you cannot look a second aorist up by its own spelling.
By whom, and through whom Two of these prepositions divide up a job English does with a single word.
Chapter 5 covered why they happen; what it could not say is how often — διά occurs 666 times and is written δι’ in 149 of them.

τὸ ῥηθὲν ὑπὸ κυρίου διὰ τοῦ προφήτου "What was spoken by the Lord through the prophet." Both prepositions inside five words, and the distinction is deliberate: the Lord is the speaker, the prophet the means.

Eight of its thirteen occurrences are distributive — ἀνὰ δύο , "two by two" (Luke 10:1); ἀνὰ δηνάριον , "a denarius each" — four of the other five are the fixed phrase ἀνὰ μέσον , "in the midst of", and the last is ἀνὰ μέρος , "in turn" (1 Corinthians 14:27).

On its own it occurs 631 times, and it heads a family of seventeen compounds worth 759 more between them: ἐξέρχομαι go out (216), εἰσέρχομαι go in (193), ἀπέρχομαι go away (117), προσέρχομαι come to (86), διέρχομαι go through (41), συνέρχομαι come together (30).

Every one.
Read the case, not only the word.

'A ransom in place of many.' ἀντί occurs only 22 times, and it is the plainest word Greek has for one thing standing where another would have stood.

ἀνά is worth a line of its own, because a lexicon will gloss it "up" and the New Testament never uses it that way.
Only περί and πρό never shorten.

δοῦναι τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ λύτρον ἀντὶ πολλῶν "To give his life a ransom in place of many." Twenty-two occurrences, and ἀντί is the plainest word Greek has for one thing standing where another would have stood.
παρά is the one preposition where all three cases are still cleanly distinct.
None of them is "up".
In chapter 5 you met four of them — ἐν, εἰς, ἐκ and ἀπό — and each one took a single case.
It occurs 193 times, and all three of its cases are still clean.
Two cases, two meanings Six prepositions carry most of this weight.
They take two cases, and two of them take three, and the case is not decoration.
Only 272 of αὐτός's 5,546 occurrences are nominative — under one in twenty.

The mnemonic worth having is that the last letter of the English word is the first letter of the Greek one: "w e " ends in an e and ἡμεῖς begins with eta, while "yo u " ends in a u and ὑμεῖς begins with upsilon.

One rule governs all of them, and it is worth having before the forms.
Of αὐτός 's 5,546 occurrences, 2,140 are genitive — nearly two in five — and most are somebody's something.

When the pronoun is emphatic A verb ending already names its subject, so a nominative pronoun is never required .

(Both of these are passives, which come later; the tense is what is in view.) τὸν καλὸν ἀγῶνα ἠγώνισμαι, τὸν δρόμον τετέλεκα, τὴν πίστιν τετήρηκα "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith." Not "I wrote it" but "it is written, and it stands".

One set of endings, two voices The primary middle and passive endings are: Primary middle/passive endings Singular Plural 1st -μαι -μεθα 2nd -σαι -σθε 3rd -ται -νται One set, and both voices use it.
Robertson's grammar said in 1915 that it "should not be used at all", and that these verbs are defective rather than deponent — a verb that never had an active has laid nothing aside.
ἔρχεται and δύναται alone are 160 of them.

So when you meet a middle, the first question is not "what is the middle voice doing here?" It is "does this verb have an active at all?" Usually it does not, and the ending is simply how the word is spelled.
Greek does this whenever an ending starting with σ meets a connecting vowel — so every second person singular in the middle looks irregular, and none of them is.
It only says that it is.
The two commonest present middle indicatives in the book are ἔρχεται (89) and δύναται (71), and neither means anything reflexive.
A different word in the middle, and 84 of the verb's 86 occurrences are middle.
One set of endings serves both, in the present, imperfect, perfect and pluperfect.
By whom, through whom, by what A passive often names the agent, and Greek has three main ways of doing it — two of them from chapter 8.
The clearest evidence that it is doing real work is a verb that means two different things in the two voices.
The exception is the second singular, and it is worth a minute now because the same thing happens in each of the next three chapters.
Middle and passive share endings in four tenses.
The form cannot tell you which is meant.
Only the verb and the sentence decide, which is why a parsing that says 'middle' is a judgement rather than a reading.
Every verb you have read so far has been active : the subject does the thing.
A verb whose two voices mean two things is the clearest evidence the middle is doing real work.
Keeping 'I am being loosed' for the present preserves the imperfective aspect and keeps the two tenses distinct.

text: μέν … δέ These two little words work as a pair, marking a contrast: μέν sets something up, and δέ answers it.
Others are frozen case forms — σήμερον, 'today', is an accusative — and adverbs never decline.
When the stem ends in a consonant These endings begin with μ, σ, τ and ν , and a stem ending in a consonant has to meet them.

With the plural article the pair means "some… others": οἱ μὲν ἦσαν σὺν τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις οἱ δὲ σὺν τοῖς ἀποστόλοις "Some were with the Jews, and others with the apostles." Both words are postpositive — they never begin their clause, and stand second.
